reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Neurocutaneous Disorders (current reference texts)
clinicalPearls: Defined by an extensive naevus sebaceus of Jadassohn, typically on the head and neck along the lines of Blaschko, in combination with cerebral, ocular and skeletal anomalies
Arises from a post-zygotic activating mosaic variant in the RAS pathway (usually HRAS, less often KRAS), so the distribution is segmental rather than generalised
Neurological features may include seizures, developmental delay, intracranial vascular or structural malformations and hemimegalencephaly on the side of the skin lesion
Ocular associations include epibulbar (limbal) dermoids, colobomas and lipodermoids, so ophthalmology review is part of the workup
Skeletal changes such as bony hypoplasia, vitamin-D-resistant hypophosphataemic rickets and limb asymmetry can accompany extensive disease
The naevus sebaceus itself carries a lifelong risk of secondary benign and malignant tumours (most often trichoblastoma, occasionally basal cell carcinoma)
Management is multidisciplinary and generic: seizure control with antiseizure therapy, surveillance of the naevus with consideration of excision, and developmental support
reference.pathophysiology: Schimmelpenning syndrome is a mosaic RASopathy caused by a post-zygotic activating variant, most commonly in HRAS and less often KRAS, occurring early in embryogenesis. Because the variant arises after fertilisation, only the clonal population of cells descended from the mutated progenitor is affected, producing lesions distributed along the lines of Blaschko. In the skin this drives an organoid naevus sebaceus with sebaceous and epidermal overgrowth, while involvement of neuroectodermal, ocular and mesodermal progenitors accounts for the associated brain, eye and skeletal anomalies. Persistent RAS-MAPK signalling within the naevus also underlies the tendency to develop secondary appendageal tumours over time.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated naevus sebaceus of Jadassohn without systemic involvement
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy to confirm naevus sebaceus and to assess any secondary tumour
MRI of the brain to detect hemimegalencephaly, structural or vascular malformations
MRA where an intracranial vascular anomaly is suspected
Ophthalmological assessment for epibulbar dermoid, coloboma and lipodermoid
Serum phosphate and skeletal survey where hypophosphataemic rickets or bony asymmetry is suspected
Molecular testing of lesional tissue for mosaic HRAS/KRAS variants where available
redFlags: New nodule, ulceration or rapid change within a naevus sebaceus suggesting secondary malignancy
Progressive neurological deficit or signs of raised intracranial pressure
Visual compromise from an ocular choristoma or coloboma
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends on the extent of extracutaneous involvement; isolated cutaneous disease has an excellent outlook, whereas extensive neurological involvement with refractory seizures and developmental delay carries a poorer prognosis, and lifelong dermatological surveillance is needed for secondary tumours.
pitfalls: Assuming an extensive naevus sebaceus is purely cosmetic and not screening for neurological, ocular or skeletal disease
Overlooking hypophosphataemic rickets as a treatable cause of skeletal symptoms
Attributing every secondary nodule to malignancy when benign trichoblastoma is more common
Delaying neuroimaging in a child presenting with seizures and a segmental head-and-neck naevus
references: Happle R. Mosaicism in Human Skin
management: Surgically excise or ablate the naevus sebaceus where cosmetically or functionally troublesome, and maintain lifelong dermatological surveillance for secondary appendageal tumours such as trichoblastoma and basal cell carcinoma
Control associated epilepsy with antiseizure medication and provide developmental and educational support for neurocognitive impairment
Refer for ophthalmological assessment and management of epibulbar dermoids, colobomas and lipodermoids
Treat hypophosphataemic (vitamin-D-resistant) rickets with oral phosphate and active vitamin D such as alfacalcidol, monitoring limb alignment and growth
Manage limb asymmetry and skeletal deformity with orthopaedic input
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across dermatology, neurology, ophthalmology, orthopaedics and clinical genetics
Counsel that the disorder arises from a post-zygotic mosaic RAS variant and is typically sporadic with low recurrence risk
